notes.meaning: Four kings from the east formed an alliance to wage war in the west. Chedorlaomer of Elam was their chief ruler, while the other three led allied regions or wandering clans. The Bible records this event as the very first war in its pages.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older scholars doubted these four kings were historical because early external records did not name them, though others suggest Amraphel was Hammurabi of Babylon.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars note that ancient Babylonian tablets from this period describe political alliances and campaigns that match the background of Genesis 14.

notes.meaning: Five rulers of city-states in the Jordan Valley joined forces to defend themselves against the eastern invaders. These five cities included the prosperous but deeply immoral towns of Sodom and Gomorrah. Their fertile lands made them an attractive target for greedy conquerors.

The five local kings gathered their armies in the Valley of Siddim, near the Dead Sea. In Abram's day this was an open, fertile plain, though it later became covered by the salty waters of the sea after God's judgment. Human greed and ambition brought all these kings into deadly conflict.

The cities of the plain had paid tribute taxes to Chedorlaomer for twelve years. In the thirteenth year, they grew tired of foreign control and chose to rebel. Their refusal to pay tribute caused the eastern kings to march west to punish them.

Chedorlaomer and his allies marched down the eastern side of the Jordan Valley in the fourteenth year to crush the rebellion. Along the way, they easily defeated several powerful peoples, including tall and fierce tribes like the Rephaites and Emites. This trail of victories showed the strength of the invading army.

The invaders continued their raid southward through the mountain area of Seir. They drove out the Horites, an ancient group known for living in hill caves, pushing them as far as the edge of the southern desert. This move prevented any southern allies from coming to help Sodom.

The eastern kings then turned northwest toward Kadesh and conquered the surrounding territories of the Amalekites and Amorites. They eliminated every rival around the Dead Sea before attacking the five rebel cities. Their sweeping march left the cities of the plain completely surrounded and without allies.

The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, and their three neighboring cities marched out into the Valley of Siddim to fight. They lined up their troops together to make a desperate stand against the invaders. Even with their united force, their easy and self-indulgent lifestyle left them unready for battle.

Four seasoned kings from the east faced off against the five kings of the plain. Although the five kings had the advantage in numbers, the four invaders were experienced fighters flushed with recent victories. Having more soldiers never guarantees safety when people turn away from God.

The Valley of Siddim was covered with deep, sticky asphalt tar pits that made running away very dangerous. When the armies of Sodom and Gomorrah broke ranks and fled, many soldiers fell into the pits, while the survivors escaped into the hills. The very ground they fought on worked against the rebel kings.

The victorious eastern kings entered Sodom and Gomorrah and stripped the cities of all their food and wealth. They carried off all the supplies like marauding desert raiders and began their journey home. Losing their food and treasure was a severe warning to people who had abused their wealth in selfish living.

The invaders captured Abram's nephew Lot and took all his belongings because he had chosen to live inside Sodom. Even though Lot was a righteous believer, he suffered alongside his corrupt neighbors when trouble struck. When God's people move close to the world, they often get caught in the world's troubles.

A survivor of the battle escaped and brought the news of Lot's capture to Abram. Abram is called 'the Hebrew,' pointing to his origin as an immigrant who crossed over the Euphrates River or to his ancestor Eber. Abram was living peacefully near Hebron under a treaty of mutual friendship with three Amorite brothers.

When Abram learned that his nephew was a prisoner, he gathered 318 armed servants born and raised in his own household. These men were trained in both personal defense and the worship of the Lord. Abram put aside past family disagreements and rushed forward out of love to save his relative.

Abram divided his small force into groups and launched a surprise attack at night. His bold strategy caught the enemy off guard in the dark, sending them running in panic past Damascus. God gave Abram courage and success against an army far larger than his own.

Abram brought back all the stolen property, his nephew Lot with all his belongings, and all the captive women and civilians. He showed kindness even to the people of Sodom, strangers he had no legal duty to help. God calls His people to show mercy and do good to all people when the chance comes.

The new king of Sodom came out to meet Abram in the King's Valley near Jerusalem after Abram returned from the battle. The ruler came to show respect and gratitude for the rescue of his citizens. God used this victory to give Abram great honor and influence in the land.

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brought out bread and wine to refresh Abram and his weary men. Salem was the early name for Jerusalem, and Melchizedek held the rare dual position of being both a king and a priest. His gift was a royal act of hospitality and fellowship after the hard fight.

differ.view: Melchizedek was a historical human king whose unique office pictured Christ, not an appearance of Jesus before His birth.
Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ Himself appearing to Abram as King and Priest.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Melchizedek's offering of bread and wine is seen as a prophetic sacrifice that prefigures the Eucharist in the Mass.

notes.meaning: Melchizedek blessed Abram in the name of God Most High, the Creator and rightful owner of heaven and earth. By giving this blessing, the priest spoke God's favor over Abram and affirmed his chosen calling. A true priest represents God to the people, and here Melchizedek reminded Abram that God rules over everything.

Melchizedek gave praise to God Most High for handing Abram victory over his enemies, and Abram gave the priest a tenth of all the plunder. A tithe is a tenth given back to God as an act of worship and thanksgiving. Abram recognized Melchizedek as a true servant of the living God and gave thanks for divine protection.

differ.view: Abram's gift shows that setting aside a tenth for God is a timeless pattern that existed before the Law of Moses.
Abram's tithe was a single offering from war spoils to honor Melchizedek's greater rank, not a binding command for Christians today.

notes.meaning: The king of Sodom told Abram to keep all the recovered goods and simply return the rescued citizens. In the customs of that time, a rescuer had the right to keep whatever plunder he won back from enemies. The king of Sodom was grateful to receive his people back, so he made a generous offer.

Abram replied that he had already lifted his hand in a solemn oath to the Lord God Most High, the Creator of heaven and earth. Raising the hand was an ancient way of making a sacred promise before God. Abram used the very titles for God that Melchizedek had just spoken, showing that he served the one true Lord of all.

Abram swore that he would not keep even a tiny thread or a sandal strap belonging to Sodom. He refused the reward so the king of Sodom could never boast that he had made Abram wealthy. Abram wanted everyone to know that his blessing and provision came from God alone.

Abram accepted only the food his young soldiers had eaten on the march and insisted that his Amorite allies receive their fair share of the plunder. Though Abram made a strict personal vow before God, he did not force that choice on his neighbors. True faith leads believers to practice personal self-denial while treating others with fairness.
